chapter_theme: The third quarter of Pattinathar's antadhi on Ekambar. The begging Lord's scenes end with the women who accuse him of coming for their waists and not for alms, and the mothers who search the street for the bangles that slipped from their daughters (904 to 907). Then a long shrine litany: Ekambar is the Lord of Kadavur, Aiyaru, Kolli, Parvatam, the Kundram hills and some forty Tevaram shrines, and every list ends by sending the hearer to Kachi (908 to 918). The last ten verses are palai love poetry: the girl elopes with the hero across the burning desert, and the foster mother, the mother, the wayfarers and the hero speak of the journey and its end in Kachi country.
structure_note: 904 to 907 continue the bhikshatana scenes of chapter 51: the women address the begging Lord (904, 905), the mothers find the street where the girls grew thin (906), and a mother notes her daughter has no signs of age yet has given her heart (907). 908 to 918 are shrine lists of the Tevaram kind, each verse a run of place names ending at Kachi Ekambam; 912 to 918 are the Kundram hills and the Chola, Nadu and Tondai shrines. 919 to 928 are the palai sequence of elopement (உடன்போக்கு): the mother's lament (919, 921, 923), the hero's company on the desert road (920, 922), the foster mother's report (924), the prayer to the sun (925), and the wayfarers who saw the pair and tell where they now are (926 to 928). Speakers are supplied from convention. From 912 the tool prints the metre field as திருவேகம்பமுடையார் instead of கட்டளைக்கலித்துறை; the metre has not changed.

904.reading: The women tell the Lord in the handsome tiger skin that his goblins hold the parasol and he came to take alms, that he took a temple in watery Kachi Ekambam where lotuses hold up a flower parasol, and that he has come here to take their waists and their garments; the waist will not break today.
904.nuance: The verse plays on கொள்ள (take): alms, a temple, a waist, a cloth. The last words இடைக்கும் இன்றே are a pun I can't fix, 'the waist (will not) give way today' or 'there is no room'. The begging Lord as a thief of women's hearts is the Thirumurai convention and is said here with the women's own mockery.

905.reading: A woman says that even today the elders' harsh words fall on the twin-breasted girl, that Kachi Ekambar whose side-glance is kind came to take alms before his bull, and asks whether this is his heart or his poison, and names it his trickery against these thick-haired women.
905.nuance: கிறித்துவம், trickery or guile, is the word the women fix on the beggar; the variant நெஞ்சம் (heart) for நஞ்சம் (poison) changes the question from 'is this your heart?' to 'is this your poison?'. தோத்த நில்லே and the middle of the verse are not clear to me.

906.reading: Speaking many cunning words, walking in the sun with his handsome form and singing many signs to take alms for Kachi Ekambar, he left the women of braided hair wasted in the long street; the mothers search there for the many white bangles that slipped away.
906.nuance: The slipped bangles (வெள்வளை போயின) are the stock sign of a woman thinned by love, and the mothers who search for them make the whole street the scene. கிறி பல பேசி, speaking cunning, carries over the women's charge from 905 into the narrator's voice.

907.reading: A mother says that in this girl the sly glance has not appeared, the words are not understood, the hair has not reached the crest, the breasts have not budded and the gem-waist has not widened, that nothing has yet come to her in the land, and yet her heart has gone to the beautiful Ekambar.
907.nuance: The repeated உற்றில (has not reached) lists the signs of womanhood that are missing, so the love is set before its season; the last line, உள்ளம் நல்கிடத்தே, may be 'in the giving of her heart' or 'as he gives her his heart'. I take it as the mother's wonder at a child's devotion.

908.reading: The one who, so that the good Brahmin of famed Kadavur might live, crushed the killing Death, himself a fierce Death; the Nectar of Maraikkadu with its cool waves, as the Mountain's daughter calls him and embraces him: the golden mountain who dwells at Kachi Ekambam amid groves.
908.nuance: The Markandeya story is given with its place, Thirukkadavur, and the Lord is called a Death to Death (கூற்றைக் குமைத்த வெங்கூற்றம்). அமிர்து is the Lord's name at Vedaranyam (Maraikkadu). This verse opens the run of shrine names that continues to 918.

909.reading: The one whom Agastya worshipped on the Malaya mountain, who sat firm on northern Kailasa for the gods to worship, who made tall Meru his bow, the lord of Thiruvekambam with green-gold walls, is the rare gem of Thiruvaiyaru girdled by the wave-tossed wide Ponni.
909.nuance: Pothiyil (Malaya) in the south and Kailasa in the north frame the Lord's range, and Aiyaru on the Kaveri is the Chola shrine; the verse makes one Lord of all of them with Ekambam as the name.

910.reading: Kolli with its gem-filled waterfalls where elephants wander dazed, Siramalai roaring with firm waterfalls, the slopes where parrots take the waterfall's spray: the mountain of Ekambar, which removes the rare karma of those who bow.
910.nuance: அருவி (waterfall) is repeated in every line, with அருவினை (rare karma) as the pun at the close; the third line's ஆல்லிந்தம் is garbled. பருப்பதம் at the end is both 'mountain' and the name of Srisailam, which 911 then names first.

911.reading: Parvatam, cloud-crawling Mandara, Indranila, the white-tusked one, Karungundram, Parangundram where he moves, Mahendra fragrant with the bowmen's fire and oblations: among all these, the one who delighted to dwell at Kachi Ekambam is our Lord.
911.nuance: The names are mythic and real mountains together, Srisailam, Mandara, Mahendra, Parankundram; வெள்ளை மருப்பு அதங்கார் and நெருப்பு அதங்கு ஆகுதி are hard to construe and may hide another name or two. The point is the choice (உகந்தான்) of Kachi among the sacred hills.

912.reading: Say these are Ekambar's hills: the bowman who shot the cities, who hid something from Himavan's good daughter: Karungundram, Venkundram, Sengundram, the king's hill, Nedungundram, long Kazhukkundram, and Mudhukundram where deeds are cut short.
912.nuance: The verse is a list of shrines whose names end in குன்றம் (hill), several of them Tevaram shrines (Kazhukkundram, Mudhukundram). மறைத்தார் ... மகட்கும் in line 2 is unclear; it may be the Lord hiding the moon or a lesson from Uma. The imperative கூறுமினே makes it a verse to be recited.

913.reading: Devotees, say Kutralam, Neyththanam, Thuruththi, Ambar; learn Velvikkudi, Thonipuram, Pazhanam; and of the Lord who set the river in his locks like lightning, Arur and Idaimarudu: so climb up, you people, thinking first of our Lord's Kachi Ekambam.
913.nuance: Three imperatives, கூறுமின், தேறுமின், ஏறுமின், turn the list into instruction; the shrines are Tevaram shrines of the Chola country, and Kachi is to be thought of first (முன் நினைந்து) before any of them.

914.reading: The Lord who gives grace to those who think of him, of Chotruthurai and Niyamam, of Pugalur, Purambiyam and Poovanam, of Venkadu with its tall palmyra groves, Pachchil and Adigai: you whose hearts give thought to him, approach Kachi Ekambam.
914.nuance: நினைவார் opens and closes the verse: the Lord graces those who think of him, and those with thinking hearts are told to come to Kachi. Thought, not pilgrimage to each place, is what the list asks for.

915.reading: Approaching and praising Avaduthurai and good Nallur, Kadambur shining on earth, Kadambanthurai, enduring Punkur, Parayththurai hard to reckon, and Ethirkolpadi of the one with the crescent garland in his locks, go and see Kachi Ekambam.
915.nuance: The verse is a plain list with the one instruction காண்மின் சென்றே, go and see; the names are Kaveri-delta shrines.

916.reading: Annamalai that climbs to reach the sky, shining Vallam, Marperu where flower honey flows, Pasur, lovely Azhundur, the gain the strong charioteer gained at Virperu, walled Otriyur: the places where the Lord of Kachi Ekambam dwells have shone.
916.nuance: வன்றேரவன் திருவிற் பெறும் பேறு may hide a shrine name (Thiruvirperu?) or refer to Arjuna gaining the bow; I can't tell. The list moves from Annamalai north into Tondai country, toward Kachi.

917.reading: Oththur of lasting fame, Amaththur, Pulivalam and Vilvalam of the one whose locks swirl with full water, Kochchai, Kondar, praised Panangadu and good Magaral: the temple of Ekambar, who gives grace to the devotees who cry 'alas' when Death comes.
917.nuance: The list ends with the Lord's act: he graces the devotees at the hour Death comes (கூற்றம் வந்தால்); the shrines are the Tondai-country Tevaram shrines around Kachi.

918.reading: Karugavur with its temple, Kachchur, Karikarai, Vanmiyur by the rising sea, Ooral, grove-filled Ponthai, Mukkonam, and Alangadu of the one garlanded with konrai: praise Ekambam.
918.nuance: The last shrine list, closing with the imperative வாழ்த்துமினே; Alangadu is the dance shrine, and Vanmiyur the sea shrine, both near Kachi.

919.reading: The mother laments that those who do not worship Ekambar of the flower anklets and the thazhai-like locks, who gives sweet grace for us to live, have gone off, if the tender feet that cannot bear the gravel desert, and the breast-burden that bends the waist of our poor flower-haired girl, are made to walk.
919.nuance: The grammar joins the shrine frame and the lament badly: either those who do not worship are the ones who took the girl into the desert, or the mother says only one who does not worship could make such feet walk. The elopement (உடன்போக்கு) begins here and runs to 928.

920.reading: A speaker tells the youth who by his generosity gained the creeper-girl who follows behind him, through the great desert where hot flame rises, to make her take it as the short cool water-field where the young of Kachi, ringed by Ekambar's cool soft-flowered groves, pluck blue lilies.
920.nuance: என்று கொளே at the close is an instruction to the hero to make the desert seem a lily pond to the girl, the palai convention of comforting the eloping woman on the road. ஆலைய பொருள் ஏகம்பனார், the Lord of the temple's wealth, is the frame.

921.reading: The mother says that to describe my doll going behind the youth through the palai, where under the burning rays the cactus flames and dried bamboos burst, as one who has forgotten even to think of the red feet of Thiruvekambar in clear-watered Kachi, is hard to say.
921.nuance: உள்ளும் அது மறந்தார் எனப் போவது உரைப்பரிதே can be read two ways: that she cannot call her daughter's going a forgetting of the Lord's feet, or that she cannot bear to tell of a going that is like forgetting them. In both, devotion to the feet is the measure of the girl's act.

922.reading: The hero tells the golden girl, like Thiruvekambam of the Lord who holds the firm Ganga on his locks, that if the forest men come with their eagle-strong force, his hot boar-like arrows will make them prey for the wing-spreading eagles, and that if he has his firm striped bow he will not hide.
922.nuance: பருந்து (eagle) is repeated in every line, and வெய்யேனம் may be a hot boar or a fierce arrow; the sense is the hero's reassurance on the robber-infested road. மறைகுவனே at the close is odd as a boast; it may be 'I will not hide' with a lost negative, or 'I will take cover'.

923.reading: The mother says that the golden goddess came to her as the grace of the king of Ekambam who wears the forest tiger's striped skin, that she gave her dice and her striped ball to the one she called her own, embraced her and left the house, and asks where she now walks on the sweet striped stony path, her faltering poor heart.
923.nuance: The gift of the toys, கழங்கு and பந்து, is the girl's farewell to childhood and the detail that carries the lament. ஒல்கும் ஏழை நெஞ்சே addresses the mother's own heart, in the Kural's manner of speaking to the heart as another.

924.reading: The foster mother reports to the friend that the girl like Kachi, of Ekambar whose anklets fill the heart with joy, has set her cotton-soft feet on the road, leaving the thorny company of the one who bore and raised her, going behind while the fearless, crackling, slaying young bull of a man goes ahead, in this world's end.
924.nuance: வெடுவெடென்ற (crackling, quick-tempered) and வையந்தத்திலே (at the world's end, or in this world) are loose; the picture, the girl behind and the fierce young man ahead, is the standard order of the eloping pair. Who speaks to whom (பாங்கி, the friend, is named) is not settled.

925.reading: The mother prays to the sun, the hot one of shining light, that there is no refuge but him to worship, Ekambar's own, in the hot silk-cotton forest, and asks him to still his wandering rays and grant grace to the girl, his fit companion, whose tender feet step on cool flowers and whose gravel is cooled as she crosses the desert.
925.nuance: The sun is addressed as the one to worship (தொழும் சரண்) and tied to Ekambar, so the prayer may treat the sun as the Lord's form, the Saiva reading, or simply ask the sun to be kind as the palai poems do. உன் உறு துணை, the companion fit for you, is the girl, perhaps because she too shines.

926.reading: Wayfarers say that like a matched pair the lovely young girl and the youth went before them, with matched breasts and matched love, and that they saw the bull-like young man fit to be embraced; and tell the deer-eyed girl to speak with this one.
926.nuance: ஒத்த (matched) four times is the verse's figure, and the last line may be the wayfarers inviting the pursuing mother to question the girl who was with them, or the pair themselves. The report of those who saw the pair on the road is the next palai stage after the lament.

927.reading: A wayfarer says that yesterday the lightning-waisted girl and the hero came to this hamlet and were seen in our house, and that those who crossed the hard hills behind them now dwell today in the Kachi country that Kambar's kings choose and worship.
927.nuance: The pair reach a settled land, and it is Kachi (கச்சி நாடு): the love poem's journey ends where the shrine poem began. The wayfarer's words to the pursuing mother are the palai convention for bringing the elopement to its safe close.

928.reading: A speaker tells the dark peacock that even when she sees Kachi, with its Siva temple whose coral towers and trident gleam in the sky, its flags tossing as if to catch the heavens, and the shrine of a thousand pillars, of Ekambar who delighted to dance in the forest the hunters call salt-barren, she should look.
928.nuance: உவரச் சொல் வேடு உடைக் காடு and அவரக்கன் போன விமானம் do not resolve; the first may be the cremation ground as a hunter's forest, the second a shrine of a thousand encircling something. The verse seems to point out the city to the arriving girl (கார் மயிலே), which fits 927's arrival in Kachi.

links.note: The bangles that slip from the wrist announce the man's parting in both: the Kural's woman asks whether her slipping bangles do not already say the lord of the shore has left; Pattinathar's mothers search the street for the white bangles that fell from the girls wasted by the begging Lord.
897 sets the Lord's right foot on the neck of thunder-voiced Death as a mark of his form; 908 tells the story behind it, the Brahmin of Kadavur saved and Death crushed, and names the place.

The Naladiyar says no one has leapt clear of Death and escaped, so give while you can; Pattinathar says the Lord crushed Death so that the Brahmin of Kadavur might live. The conflict holds if the Markandeya story is taken as a claim that one man did escape; if the Naladiyar speaks of ordinary men and the verse of a miracle, they need not clash.

Both say Death can be leapt past: the Kural's one who has the power of austerity can; Pattinathar's Brahmin of Kadavur lived because the Lord crushed Death. The Kural credits tapas, Pattinathar the Lord's act for a devotee.

Tirumular makes the heart the temple and the body the shrine; Pattinathar lists a dozen shrines and then tells those with thinking hearts (நினைவார் தரு நெஞ்சினீர்) to come to Kachi. The thinking heart is the condition in both, but Pattinathar still sends it to a place, which Tirumular's verse makes unnecessary.

Both speak to the heart as a separate party in a parting: the Kural's woman's heart climbs at the thought of the man's return; Pattinathar's mother asks her faltering poor heart where the eloped girl now walks on the stony path. The love is a lover's in one and a mother's in the other.

source_issues: 912 to 928 have the metre field printed as திருவேகம்பமுடையார் (the work's name) instead of கட்டளைக்கலித்துறை; the verses are in the same metre as the rest.
910 line 4 reads ஏகமபர் for ஏகம்பர், and line 3's ஆல்லிந்தம் is garbled.
904 line 4 has a space inside வந் தீரிடைக்குமின்றே, apparently வந்தீர் இடைக்கும் இன்றே.
905 has a variant note நெஞ்சங்கிதுவோ for நஞ்சங்கிதுவோ, and the printed line has a space inside தோத்த நஞ்சங்கிதுவோ.
The shrine names in 911, 912 and 916 are partly unparsed; some words I could not assign to a known shrine.
